title: Preference versus performance: Investigating the dissociation between objective measures and subjective ratings of usability for schematic metro maps and intuitive theories of design
research_question: To investigate the dissociation between objective performance measures (journey planning time) and subjective ratings (usability, attractiveness, preference) for different schematic metro map designs, and to explore underlying intuitive theories of design.

participants.description:
Experiment 1: 80 subjects (28 males, 52 females, mean age 22.0 years, SD 4.9). Residents of Essex or adjacent counties, majority unfamiliar with Paris Metro network.
Experiment 2: 649 respondents (541 male, 108 female, mean age 36.2 years, SD 14.3). 290 from UK, 118 from USA/Canada, 116 from Germany.
Experiment 3: 72 subjects (27 males, 45 females, mean age 35.9 years, SD 13.0). Majority unfamiliar with Berlin.
participants.recruitment:
Experiment 1 & 3: Acquaintances of experimenters, unpaid volunteers (Exp 1 also students receiving £5.00).
Experiment 2: Recruited via map-related newsletter and recommendations via various map-related websites.

stimuli_or_exposures.description:
Experiment 1: Two Paris Metro maps (official RATP octolinear design, novel curvilinear design). Both A3 laminated sheets.
Experiment 2: Nine London Underground maps (3 design rules: octolinear, multilinear, curvilinear; 3 design priorities: stylised, geographical, compact). Presented as thumbnails with pop-up large versions.
Experiment 3: Three Berlin U-/S-Bahn maps (octolinear, curvilinear, multilinear), all optimized for simplified line trajectories. A3 laminated sheets. Also, the three stylised London Underground maps from Experiment 2 for comparison.
Experiment 2: Nine London Underground maps (3 design rules: octolinear, multilinear, curvilinear; 3 design priorities: stylised, geographical, compact).
Experiment 3: Three Berlin U-/S-Bahn maps (octolinear, curvilinear, multilinear), all optimized for simplified line trajectories.

measures.instrument: Calculated based on 2 minutes per station and 10 minutes per interchange
Number of invalid routes (interchanges not designated)
19-item questionnaire (Exp 1), 24-item questionnaire (Exp 3), 7-point/5-point Likert scales, aggregate score
Classification based on consistent patterns of usability ratings across maps

mechanisms: Dissociation between objective performance and subjective ratings: Metacognitive failures due to limited salient cues for performance differences, leading users to evaluate maps based on superficial properties, expectations, and prejudices rather than actual usability.

Familiarity-liking effect / Fluency framework: Repeated exposure and familiarity with octolinear designs lead to perceived easier cognitive processing and positive evaluations, even if not objectively more usable.

Intuitive theories of design: Pre-existing beliefs or schemas about what constitutes effective map design (e.g., octolinearity, simplicity) influence subjective ratings and choices, often overriding objective performance.
Intrinsic preference for curved objects: Curvilinear maps may be rated more attractive due to an innate aesthetic preference for curved shapes over awkwardly angled ones.
Reduced octolinear bias for unfamiliar cities: For less familiar networks, the strong expectation for octolinear designs is weaker, allowing attractiveness to drive usability judgments more strongly.
implementation_implications: Objective usability testing is crucial for identifying effective schematic map designs, as subjective ratings and public preferences are often uncorrelated with actual performance.
Designers should experiment with alternative design rules beyond octolinearity, optimizing for simplicity and coherence, especially for networks where octolinearity is incompatible with structure.
Automation of schematic map production should incorporate algorithms that can generate maps with different linearity levels, optimized for various usability criteria.

User acceptance is important, but if a bias towards certain design rules is purely familiarity-based without objective usability benefits, it may prevent the adoption of more effective unconventional designs.
For unfamiliar cities/networks, curvilinear designs may achieve greater user acceptance than multilinear ones due to higher attractiveness ratings, even if objective performance is similar.

limitations: The sample in Experiment 2 cannot be said to be representative of the general population due to recruitment methods.
The restricted age range for Experiment 1 precluded identifying any substantial relationships between age and other variables.
The within-subjects design runs the risk of item effects and cross-talk between maps, though analysis suggested these were not problematic for overall interpretations.
The study did not provide subjects with feedback on their performance, which might have influenced the dissociation between objective and subjective measures.
The study did not explicitly investigate whether subjects' estimates of journey duration or planning time would bridge the objective-subjective gap.
The London network is not ideal for usability studies requiring many complex two-interchange journeys due to its high interconnectedness.
The generalisability of findings regarding intuitive theories of design is limited to the current context.
